Newborn Care

Dehydration in babies: signs, feeding and getting help

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A baby can become dehydrated when fluid intake does not replace losses. This can happen through poor milk transfer, vomiting, diarrhoea, fever or heat, sometimes with more than one cause. Young infants can deteriorate quickly: the priority is recognising a change and getting the right assessment, rather than choosing a drink from a general children’s guide.

Get help early for a young baby

Seek urgent medical advice if your baby takes much less milk, has fewer wet nappies than usual, has a dry mouth, sunken eyes or a sunken soft spot, produces fewer tears, or seems unusually drowsy or irritable. A baby under six months with suspected dehydration should be assessed by a clinician. Do not wait for vomiting, diarrhoea or every sign to appear.

A baby who stops feeding or cannot keep fluids down also needs prompt assessment. Tell the service the baby’s exact age, when feeding and urine last occurred, and any illness or heat exposure. Do not wait for eight hours of diarrhoea, two consecutive vomits or a particular nappy total before asking for help.

Recognise emergency signs

Get emergency help now if your baby is difficult to wake, cannot be woken, faints, has a seizure, has difficulty breathing or very fast breathing, or has blue, grey, unusually pale or blotchy skin. Skin that feels cold or damp, a rash that does not fade when pressed, or a weak, high-pitched or continuous cry also needs immediate emergency assessment. These are separate warning signs; they need not occur together.

A temperature of 38°C or higher under three months, 39°C or higher at three to six months, or below 36°C needs immediate medical assessment. No urine for twelve hours, green or yellow-green vomit, blood or coffee-ground-like material in vomit, or sudden severe tummy pain also warrants emergency care. Seek help sooner if the baby is unwell; twelve hours is not a waiting target. Follow local emergency instructions and never force a feed into a baby who cannot stay awake or swallow safely.

Why babies lose their fluid balance

Milk normally replaces water lost in urine, stools, breathing and through the skin. Dehydration develops when too little is taken in, too much is lost, or both. It can disturb salts in the blood as well as circulation; severe dehydration can be life-threatening. A fixed percentage of body water does not tell you how ill an individual baby is.

Infants depend on adults for feeds and cannot explain thirst. Those under six months, babies born small, and babies with particular heart, kidney or other medical conditions need extra caution. Tell the clinician about medicines and any special feeding plan; ordinary home advice may not fit those circumstances.

Look at nappies, feeding and behaviour together

A fall from your baby’s usual urine output, darker urine, dry lips or mouth, sunken eyes or soft spot, fewer tears and a change in alertness can suggest dehydration. No single sign reliably measures its severity. A baby can have an early fluid deficit without every visible sign, and counting nappies does not replace a clinical assessment.

The first days after birth are different: small urine amounts increase as milk intake rises. NHS breastfeeding guidance describes only two or three wet nappies in the first 48 hours, rising to at least six heavy wet nappies in 24 hours from day five. Use the baby’s age, feeding plan and overall condition; do not apply six nappies from birth or assume a reassuring count rules out illness.

Consider inadequate milk intake

A baby may spend time at the breast without transferring enough milk, or have difficulty attaching, sucking or staying awake to feed. Milk production may also be insufficient. With bottle feeding, the amount offered, preparation, flow and the baby’s ability to drink all matter. Poor intake is a reason for practical help, not parental blame.

Ask a trained professional to observe a complete breast or bottle feed and review swallowing, attachment, intake and weight. Newborn weight loss needs interpretation: more than 10% of birth weight is a reason for assessment and feeding support, not a target to wait for. An ill or poorly feeding baby needs help even with a smaller loss.

Illness and heat can increase losses

Vomiting and watery diarrhoea can remove fluid and salts while also reducing appetite. Fever, a hot environment, mouth pain or a blocked nose can interfere with intake or increase losses. Dehydration can occur without a stomach bug, and reduced feeding can be a sign of a more serious illness.

Do not explain substantial refusal, diarrhoea or a sick appearance away as teething. Move an overheated baby to a cooler place and remove unnecessary layers while arranging care when needed. Cooling alone does not rule out infection or treat severe dehydration, and a young infant’s fever still needs assessment.

What the clinician checks

Assessment brings together age, previous and current weight, milk intake, urine, stools, vomiting, temperature and examination. The clinician checks circulation, breathing, responsiveness and signs of the underlying cause. A recent reliable weight can be useful, but do not delay care to obtain a home weight or try to calculate a dehydration percentage yourself.

Blood tests are not necessary for every mild episode. Glucose and blood salts may need checking in a young infant with poor feeding or large losses, severe dehydration, unusual symptoms or a need for intravenous fluids. A high sodium level can require carefully controlled replacement; this cannot be judged from urine colour or treated by rapidly giving extra water at home.

Build a safe milk-feeding plan

Continue breastfeeding when the baby is alert enough to feed safely, including during most vomiting or diarrhoea illnesses. Smaller, more frequent feeds can help, but a rigid twenty-minute feed every two hours does not prove adequate intake. A sleepy baby who cannot feed effectively needs assessment, not simply more scheduled attempts.

If extra milk is needed, the team may recommend expressed milk, formula or a combination, with quantities and review tailored to the baby. Support for expressing and attachment can help preserve breastfeeding if that is your wish. Do not delay needed supplementation out of fear that accepting help means breastfeeding has failed.

Prepare formula at the intended strength

Use the exact water-to-formula ratio on the product label and any specialist instructions. Too little water can contribute to dehydration; extra water reduces nutrition and can upset the baby’s fluid and salt balance. Ready-to-feed formula does not need water added. Never concentrate or dilute a feed to treat dehydration yourself.

Use safe water and clean hands and feeding equipment, following local preparation and storage advice. Tell the clinician if a mixing error may have occurred and bring the product details. Replacing milk with water, juice, fizzy drinks or a homemade formula is not a safe general solution for a young infant.

When oral rehydration solution is appropriate

Oral rehydration solution (ORS) replaces water and salts in a controlled mixture. It can be part of treatment for dehydration from diarrhoea or vomiting, including in infants, but a young baby needs a clinician-directed plan. Ask which product, how much, how often and when to reassess; a general older-child recipe is not an infant prescription.

Mix a powder with exactly the amount of safe water specified; do not add juice, sugar or extra powder. Give small frequent amounts only as advised and only when the baby can swallow safely. Breastfeeding usually continues. During active rehydration, follow the team’s instructions about other milk feeds and food; after rehydration, usual full-strength milk and age-appropriate food can resume. Persistent vomiting or refusal of ORS needs reassessment.

Understand when hospital treatment is needed

Severe dehydration, shock, deterioration or inability to manage fluids safely may require hospital care. Some babies can receive fluid through a tube into the stomach; others need an intravenous drip. Staff monitor response, ongoing losses and blood results where necessary, and treat the cause as well as replacing fluid.

Antibiotics are not routine for a viral stomach bug, though some infections need specific treatment. Do not give anti-diarrhoea medicine or an anti-vomiting medicine to a baby without prescribing advice. Ask before using pain or fever medicines when dehydration is suspected, particularly ibuprofen; medicine must not delay assessment.

Extra water depends on age and context

For a well exclusively breastfed baby under about six months, extra breastfeeds generally supply fluid needs even in hot weather. Formula remains correctly mixed. UK advice allows small amounts of cooled boiled water for formula-fed babies in hot weather, while advice elsewhere may differ. Ask your local child-health professional what fits your baby; this is different from treating suspected dehydration.

Around six months, water can be offered with complementary foods while breast milk or formula remains important. Do not substitute large water feeds for milk or improvise a salt-and-sugar mixture. A baby who is already dehydrated needs assessment and an appropriate replacement plan, not just permission to drink water.

Reduce the chance of another episode

Offer feeds responsively and follow any individual plan for waking to feed, supplementation and weight review. Protect babies from excessive heat, keep young babies out of direct sun, avoid too many layers and never leave a baby in a parked car. A blanket over a pram can trap heat; use a suitable shade with airflow.

Wash hands with soap and water before preparing feeds and after nappy changes, and clean feeding equipment as instructed. People with vomiting or diarrhoea should avoid preparing the baby’s feeds when possible. These measures reduce infection risk but do not guarantee prevention; continue monitoring feeding during any illness.

Agree on follow-up and what to record

Before going home, ask for a clear plan: feeds or ORS, what improvement to expect, the next review and who to contact if things worsen. Record approximate feeds, vomiting or loose stools, wet nappies, temperature and medicines. Keep checking responsiveness and feeding, including overnight when the baby is unwell.

More urine or a better feed can be encouraging, but persistent poor intake, recurrent symptoms or an infant who is not returning to their usual behaviour deserves reassessment. Attend planned weight and feeding checks. If access to milk, equipment, transport or help is difficult, tell the team so the plan is workable rather than relying on willpower.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Seek early assessment for a young infant with a change in feeding, urine or alertness.

Ask for an individual milk or ORS plan and clear emergency and follow-up instructions.

Bring feeding, nappy, illness and preparation details without delaying urgent care.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise feed, nappy and appointment notes. It cannot diagnose dehydration, grade its severity, prescribe fluid volumes or decide that an unwell baby can wait.

When to seek help

Suspected dehydration in a baby under six months needs clinical assessment. Get emergency help for difficulty waking, fainting, seizures, breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, abnormal blue/grey/pale/blotchy colour, cold or damp skin, a non-fading rash or an abnormal cry. High temperature at the age thresholds described above, temperature below 36°C, twelve hours without urine, green or bloody vomit or sudden severe pain also needs immediate assessment. Do not wait for every sign or force fluids into an unsafe swallow. Never dilute formula.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Young infants with suspected dehydration need early clinical assessment.
  • Check feeding, urine and behaviour together; no nappy number rules out illness.
  • Continue safe milk feeds and use ORS only within an appropriate infant care plan.
  • Never change formula concentration or use large water feeds as a treatment.
  • Breathing, colour or responsiveness changes and other emergency signs must not wait.

Frequently asked questions

Can dehydration happen without diarrhoea?

Yes. Inadequate milk transfer or intake, vomiting, fever, heat and other illnesses can contribute. A baby does not need a stomach bug to require assessment.

Does every newborn need six wet nappies from birth?

No. Output changes during the first days. NHS guidance describes at least six heavy wet nappies a day from day five, with fewer earlier. A drop in output or an unwell baby needs advice regardless of the count.

Should I wait until the soft spot is deeply sunken?

No. Reduced feeding or urine, a dry mouth, a sunken soft spot or eyes, fewer tears or unusual drowsiness or irritability already warrants urgent advice. A baby under six months with suspected dehydration should see a clinician.

Should breastfeeding stop during vomiting or diarrhoea?

Usually not. Continue when the baby can feed safely and follow the treatment plan. Inability to stay awake, swallow safely or keep fluids down needs urgent help, not repeated forced feeds.

Can I use ORS for a baby?

It may be appropriate, but young infants need a clinician-directed product, amount and review plan. Mix it exactly as instructed and do not substitute juice, fizzy drinks or a homemade mixture.

Should I dilute formula or give a bottle of water?

Do not dilute formula. Extra water advice depends on age, feeding and conditions; it is not a treatment plan for a dehydrated young infant. Seek assessment and individual advice.

Will every dehydrated baby need a drip?

No. The route depends on severity, cause and ability to tolerate fluids. Oral treatment or a stomach tube may be suitable; severe dehydration, shock or failure of that approach can require intravenous treatment and monitoring.

Which changes mean emergency help now?

Difficulty waking, fainting, a seizure, breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue/grey/pale/blotchy skin, cold or damp skin, a non-fading rash or an abnormal weak/high-pitched/continuous cry are independent emergency signs. Age-specific high or very low temperature, no urine for twelve hours, green/yellow-green or bloody vomit, or sudden severe tummy pain also needs immediate assessment. Do not wait for all signs or for twelve hours to pass if the baby is unwell.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
